questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient undergoing general anesthesia develops left lung collapse following intubation. On auscultation, breath sounds are heard only on the right side. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
options: Pneumothorax on the left side due to positive pressure ventilation
Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
questions.concept: If the endotracheal tube is advanced too far it usually enters the more vertical right main bronchus, ventilating only the right lung, so breath sounds are heard on the right with left-lung collapse. Withdrawing the tube restores bilateral ventilation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient under anesthesia is found to be in a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate (CICV) scenario. What is the next best step in management?
questions.concept: In a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate emergency an immediate surgical airway is required; cricothyroidotomy is the fastest and most accessible option (incision through the cricothyroid membrane) and is preferred over the slower tracheostomy. An NPA is only an adjunct and an LMA has already failed by this point.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: After a road traffic accident, a patient has severe maxillofacial trauma with SpO2 80% on room air and cannot be intubated or ventilated. What is your immediate step?
options: Do suction and again try intubation
questions.concept: Severe maxillofacial trauma with a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate state and desaturation is an indication for an emergency surgical airway; cricothyrotomy provides oxygenation within seconds and is preferred over the slower tracheostomy or re-attempting intubation in a rapidly desaturating patient.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: According to the American Heart Association (AHA), what is the 6th link added to the chain of survival?
questions.concept: The AHA Chain of Survival gained a sixth link, Recovery (and rehabilitation), recognising that care continues beyond return of spontaneous circulation. Rapid defibrillation and high-quality CPR are earlier, pre-existing links.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In epidural anesthesia, which of the following layers is least likely to be punctured during the procedure?
questions.concept: In an epidural the needle stops in the epidural (extradural) space, so it crosses skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and ligamentum flavum but does NOT pierce the dura or arachnoid mater; arachnoid puncture occurs only in spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia. (Option D 'Infraspinous' is a mis-transcription of the interspinous ligament.)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painful, red, granular lesion on the vulva accompanied by bilateral lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A painful, soft, granular genital ulcer with painful (often suppurative) inguinal lymphadenopathy is characteristic of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; painless ulcers instead suggest syphilis (indurated) or granuloma inguinale (beefy-red, Donovan bodies, no nodes).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old presents with flaccid blisters and painful oral erosions; lateral pressure on normal-looking skin shears off the epidermis (Nikolsky's sign positive). Which set of findings correctly fits pemphigus vulgaris (rather than bullous pemphigoid)?
options: Intraepidermal (suprabasal) blister, Nikolsky positive, IgG against desmoglein 3
Intraepidermal blister, Nikolsky negative, no autoantibodies
Subepidermal blister, Nikolsky negative, IgG against BP180/BP230
Subepidermal blister, linear IgA at the basement membrane
questions.concept: Pemphigus vulgaris: intraepidermal (suprabasal) acantholytic blister, flaccid bullae, Nikolsky positive, autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (with a 'fish-net' intercellular IgG pattern on direct immunofluorescence). Bullous pemphigoid: tense subepidermal blisters, Nikolsky negative, antibodies against hemidesmosomal BP180/BP230 with linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy develops a reaction with a visibly thickened nerve in the neck. Which hypersensitivity type and which enlarged nerve are involved?
questions.concept: A type 1 (reversal) leprosy reaction is a delayed, cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, and the greater auricular nerve is the classic thickened nerve palpable in the neck. (The type 2 reaction / erythema nodosum leprosum is instead an immune-complex, type III phenomenon.) Hence type IV plus the greater auricular nerve.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which of the following drug dosages is incorrect for the treatment of leprosy in adults?
questions.concept: In WHO MDT for adult leprosy rifampicin is 600 mg once monthly (450 mg is the child dose), so 'rifampicin 450 mg' is the wrong adult dose. Dapsone 100 mg daily, clofazimine 300 mg monthly plus 50 mg daily are all correct.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A child with a sore throat starts developing skin lesions as in the image below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Guttate psoriasis appears as sudden crops of small, drop-like (guttate) scaly papules a week or two after a streptococcal sore throat, classically in children and young adults; the post-strep history is the key pointer even without the image.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: What is the most commonly used test for newborn hearing screening?
questions.concept: Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) are the standard first-line universal newborn hearing screen - quick, non-invasive and objective; BERA is used as the confirmatory second-tier test in babies who fail OAE.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient presents to the OPD with hearing loss. On examination: Rinne test- Positive in the left ear and negative in the right ear; Weber's test - lateralization towards the left; Bone conduction test - Reduced in the right ear and similar in the left ear. Interpret the findings.
options: Conductive hearing loss in left ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in left ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in right ear
Conductive hearing loss in right ear
questions.concept: Reduced bone conduction on the right and Weber lateralising to the left (better) ear indicate right sensorineural hearing loss; the right Rinne-negative result is a 'false-negative Rinne', seen in severe unilateral SNHL because the fork's bone-conducted sound is heard by the opposite normal cochlea.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presented with ear discharge and severe itching in the ear since 7 days. On examination, a wet newspaper appearance was seen as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: The 'wet newspaper' appearance with severe itching and discharge in the external auditory canal is otomycosis, usually due to Aspergillus niger (black fungal spores) or Candida; treatment is aural toilet plus a topical antifungal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presented with fever, pain and swelling over the mastoid with forward displacement of the pinna. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Postauricular swelling and tenderness with downward-and-forward displacement of the pinna is the classic sign of acute mastoiditis, a suppurative complication of acute otitis media. Bezold abscess tracks into the neck along sternocleidomastoid; Citelli abscess is posterior/occipital.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A patient with a history of trauma presents with hearing loss. A High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) scan was performed. Which of the following structures is not typically visualized on HRCT?
questions.concept: HRCT of the temporal bone resolves bony and air-containing structures (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals) but cannot show the microscopic soft-tissue organ of Corti within the cochlear duct.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A tympanometry graph shows a shallow peak at pressure = 0 daPa. What is the most likely diagnosis based on this tympanometry result?
questions.concept: A tympanogram with the peak at normal (0 daPa) pressure but reduced (shallow) compliance is Type As, indicating a stiffened/fixed ossicular system such as otosclerosis or tympanosclerosis. Type A is normal, Type B is flat (effusion), and Type Ad is a very tall peak (ossicular discontinuity).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male was admitted with respiratory distress. CT showed a nasal polyp with fluid collection in the sinus. Drainage of which of the following is obstructed?
questions.concept: The maxillary sinus drains through an ostium placed high on its medial wall into the middle meatus, so it drains poorly and readily retains fluid; antrochoanal polyps also classically arise from the maxillary antrum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: The upper part of the uncinate process commonly attaches to?
questions.concept: The uncinate process is a hook-shaped ethmoid bony leaflet of the lateral nasal wall whose upper end most commonly attaches to the middle turbinate; with the ethmoid bulla it bounds the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus. (Its superior attachment is variable, but the middle turbinate is the textbook answer.)

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A 49-year-old female from Nagaland presented with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. On examination, dull tympanic membrane with lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck was seen. Which of the following is the management for the condition?
questions.concept: Unilateral serous otitis media (dull TM, conductive loss from Eustachian-tube blockage), tinnitus and posterior-triangle cervical nodes in a patient from north-east India point to nasopharyngeal carcinoma; it is radiosensitive, so radiotherapy is the mainstay.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.stem: A purely glottic (true vocal cord) carcinoma of the larynx typically presents early and carries the best prognosis among laryngeal cancers. Which anatomical feature best explains both the early presentation and the good prognosis?
options: The glottis has a rich lymphatic supply causing early symptomatic nodes
The true vocal cords have sparse lymphatic drainage and hoarseness appears early
The supraglottis has no lymphatic drainage at all
The subglottis presents earliest, with stridor
questions.concept: The true vocal cords have very poor lymphatic drainage, so glottic cancers spread to nodes late (good prognosis) while causing hoarseness early (early presentation). Supraglottic tumours have rich lymphatics and therefore metastasise to nodes early with a worse prognosis.
questions.reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with a history of throat infection presents with a water hammer pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A collapsing 'water-hammer' (Corrigan) pulse signifies aortic regurgitation, and a preceding sore throat points to post-streptococcal rheumatic fever as the underlying cause - so rheumatic aortic regurgitation is the best fit.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 30% remains breathless (NYHA class II-III) despite an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker at target doses, with potassium 4.4 mmol/L and normal renal function. Which additional class has the best evidence for reducing MORTALITY in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
questions.concept: In HFrEF, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone) reduce mortality when added to an ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker (RALES/EMPHASIS-HF). Loop diuretics relieve congestion but have no proven mortality benefit; digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21e - Heart Failure: Management

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with chronic stable angina presents with worsening chest pain during routine activities. His current medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and atorvastatin, but his symptoms persist. ECG shows ST-segment depression in V5-V6, and coronary angiography reveals 80% stenosis of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent (DES)
Refer for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)
questions.concept: For chronic stable angina with limiting symptoms despite optimal medical therapy and a significant single-vessel stenosis (80% LAD), PCI with a drug-eluting stent is the best next step; CABG is reserved for left-main, multivessel, or LV-dysfunction/diabetic disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with known rheumatic heart disease is found to have a 1-2 cm aneurysm on imaging. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.concept: A large (10-20 mm) coronary artery aneurysm carries a high risk of thrombosis, embolisation and MI, so long-term (lifelong) low-dose aspirin is the mainstay of antithrombotic prophylaxis; dual antiplatelets are reserved for giant aneurysms or acute events. NOTE: the recalled stem says 'rheumatic heart disease' but the explanation clearly concerns a coronary artery aneurysm (Kawasaki-type management), which appears to be a recall/extraction artifact; answer A holds for a large coronary aneurysm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient develops a broad-QRS-complex tachycardia after an MI. His BP is 120/85 mmHg and he is haemodynamically stable. What is the best management?
questions.concept: A haemodynamically stable wide-QRS tachycardia after MI is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, for which IV amiodarone is the appropriate pharmacologic choice. Nitroglycerin and beta-blockers (metoprolol/labetalol) do not terminate VT and could worsen the situation. (The source gave no explanation; the answer is confirmed on standard ACLS grounds.)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with a past history of heart disease presents with central chest pain. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads (V2-V4) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6), with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads (III, aVF). What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: ST elevation spanning the anterior (V2-V4) and lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6) leads localises injury to the anterolateral wall (LAD +/- LCX/diagonal territory). The reciprocal inferior ST depression confirms acute MI and argues against pericarditis, which shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal changes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A hypertensive patient's lab results reveal hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (and high-to-normal sodium) is primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia: aldosterone drives Na+ retention with renal K+ and H+ loss. Addison's disease is the mirror image (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes presents for a routine follow-up. Her serum creatinine and potassium levels are normal, but she has microalbuminuria and an HbA1c of 8%. Her blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits, and she is currently on metformin for diabetes management. What should be the next step in her management?
options: Stop Metformin and start a different OHA
questions.concept: In type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is the next step - it slows progression of diabetic nephropathy and lowers cardiovascular risk even when blood pressure is normal (monitor potassium and creatinine).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism behind tissue damage in long-standing diabetes?
questions.concept: Chronic hyperglycaemia is the fundamental driver of diabetic tissue injury, acting through advanced glycation end-products, the polyol (sorbitol) pathway, protein kinase C activation and the hexosamine pathway. Sorbitol accumulation is only one downstream arm, not the primary mechanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 23-year-old female visited the clinician with a solitary thyroid nodule and was advised for thyroid function tests where Tsh level is 27.3mU/L, T3 is 1.24 ng/ml, and T4 is 4.87 microgram/ml. Which of the following manifestations is true regarding the condition?
questions.concept: An elevated TSH with low/low-normal T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism, which slows metabolism and causes weight gain; heat intolerance, tachycardia and diarrhoea are hyperthyroid features.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with hypercalcemia, bone pain, renal stones, and abdominal pain. Which condition is most likely?
questions.concept: Hypercalcaemia with 'bones (pain), stones (renal calculi), abdominal groans and psychic moans' is the picture of primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a parathyroid adenoma secreting excess PTH, which mobilises calcium from bone and increases renal calcium reabsorption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair and dry skin and is diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which antibody is characteristically seen?
questions.concept: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune hypothyroidism) is marked by anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which drive autoimmune destruction of the gland. The long-acting thyroid stimulator (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin) belongs to Graves' disease, causing hyperthyroidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What condition is likely in a newborn presenting with dry, rough skin, a big tongue and rough hair?
questions.concept: A neonate with coarse dry skin, macroglossia (large tongue), coarse hair, hypotonia and prolonged jaundice suggests congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism); untreated it causes irreversible intellectual disability, which is why newborn TSH screening exists.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with tremors, weight loss, heat intolerance, and palpitations. Which hormone is most likely elevated?
questions.concept: Tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance and palpitations are features of thyrotoxicosis from elevated thyroid hormone (T4/T3), which raises basal metabolic rate and up-regulates beta-adrenergic sensitivity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, difficulty in speech, and behavioral changes. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and a golden-brown ring at the limbus of the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring). Wilson's disease is suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Wilson's disease is confirmed most specifically by quantitative hepatic copper on liver biopsy (the gold standard, >250 ug/g dry weight). NOTE: low serum ceruloplasmin is the best initial screening test and 24-h urinary copper is raised, but liver-biopsy copper is the definitive confirmatory investigation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A man with alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites develops fever, diffuse abdominal pain and worsening encephalopathy. A diagnostic ascitic tap shows 480 polymorphonuclear cells/mm3 with no surgical source on imaging. Besides IV cefotaxime, which intervention reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival?
options: Immediate large-volume paracentesis of all the ascites
questions.concept: An ascitic PMN count of 250/mm3 or more diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; treatment is a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) PLUS IV albumin (typically on day 1 and day 3), which reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Rifaximin/lactulose treat encephalopathy, not SBP; FFP is not indicated without active bleeding.
questions.reference: Harrison's 21e - Cirrhosis and its Complications (Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 38-year-old male presents with a one-week history of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia. Skin examination reveals multiple purpura and petechiae on the left shoulder, trunk, and legs. Similar cases have been reported linked to increased incidence of mosquito breeding. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?
questions.concept: The picture (fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, petechiae/purpura in a mosquito-breeding outbreak) is dengue; its commonest neurological complication is dengue encephalopathy (typically in DHF/DSS, with normal CSF), rather than true encephalitis, GBS or stroke.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Following the recent Mumbai floods, a 28-year-old male laborer presents with high-grade fever, severe calf muscle tenderness, and conjunctival suffusion. He reports walking through stagnant water contaminated with rodent excreta. Dark-field microscopy reveals highly motile, tightly coiled spiral organisms with hooked ends. What is the causative pathogen?
questions.concept: Fever with severe calf-muscle tenderness, conjunctival suffusion, and exposure to flood water contaminated by rodent urine, plus tightly coiled hook-ended spirochetes on dark-field microscopy, is leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.concept: A high pH (7.5) with a raised HCO3- (33) is a metabolic alkalosis, and the modestly raised pCO2 (48) is appropriate respiratory compensation. Recurrent vomiting causes it by loss of gastric H+ (with chloride, potassium and volume depletion).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient develops renal shutdown after a road traffic accident. Workup shows FeNa < 1%, urine osmolality 300 mOsm/kg and urinary sodium 40 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A urine sodium of about 40 mEq/L with isosthenuric urine (osmolality ~300, similar to plasma) reflects failed tubular sodium reabsorption and concentration, i.e. acute tubular necrosis rather than pre-renal AKI (which shows urine Na <20 and osmolality >500). NOTE: the quoted FeNa <1% is atypical for ATN and would fit pre-renal, but a low FeNa is a recognised exception in early/pigment-induced ATN, and the high urine Na plus isosthenuria point to ATN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with electrical burns and stable vitals is noted to have red-coloured urine. What is the most likely finding in this patient's blood?
questions.concept: Electrical burns cause deep muscle necrosis and rhabdomyolysis; released myoglobin turns the urine red and released intracellular potassium produces hyperkalaemia (with risk of myoglobinuric acute kidney injury). The red urine is myoglobinuria, not true haematuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with severe burns develops hemoglobinuria and acute renal failure. Which pigment is responsible?
questions.concept: Pigment-induced acute kidney injury after major burns occurs when heme pigment precipitates in and is directly toxic to renal tubules. NOTE: the stem says 'haemoglobinuria' (which would make haemoglobin the pigment), but haemoglobin is NOT among the options; the recall key gives myoglobin (from associated rhabdomyolysis/deep muscle injury). The item is internally inconsistent, so it is flagged verified:N: teach the general concept of pigment nephropathy rather than relying on this key.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 12-year-old child is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy reveals wire-loop lesions. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this case?
questions.concept: Wire-loop lesions with nephrotic-range proteinuria indicate diffuse proliferative (Class IV) lupus nephritis, whose standard induction therapy is high-dose corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide (mycophenolate mofetil is an accepted alternative induction agent).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient in circulatory failure has ABG values: pH 7.3, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, pCO2 25 mmHg. What is the acid-base status?
options: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
questions.concept: Low pH with low HCO3- is a metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis from shock). Winter's formula (expected pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3- + 8 +/- 2 = 23 +/- 2) matches the measured pCO2 of 25, so respiratory compensation is appropriate: a simple metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with a history of vomiting. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals pH 7.5, pCO2 48 mm Hg and HCO3- 30 mmol/L. What is the most likely acid-base abnormality?
questions.concept: An alkalaemic pH (7.5) with a raised bicarbonate (30) is a primary metabolic alkalosis; here it results from loss of gastric HCl during vomiting, and the raised pCO2 (48) reflects appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has chronic hypercalcemia for 1.5 years but a normal PTH level. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: Chronic, stable hypercalcaemia with a normal PTH is PTH-independent; in a young man this fits sarcoidosis, where granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase and make excess calcitriol. Parathyroid hyperplasia would raise PTH and CKD tends to lower calcium. NOTE: malignancy is the commonest PTH-independent cause overall, but its hypercalcaemia is usually acute with weight loss, so the chronic stable course here favours sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A child was brought to the casualty with complaints of vomiting and loose stools with a history of laxative use. On examination, arrhythmia is present. What will be the abnormality present?
questions.concept: Vomiting, diarrhoea and laxative abuse all cause gastrointestinal potassium loss; the resulting hypokalaemia is the electrolyte disturbance that precipitates cardiac arrhythmias. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval but is not the primary abnormality here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea and is diagnosed with GBS. What is the cause?
questions.concept: GBS is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy (often post-Campylobacter diarrhoea) that strikes myelinated peripheral nerve fibres, producing ascending weakness and areflexia; it is a peripheral nerve/root process, not spinal-cord demyelination or cord inflammation. NOTE: the option wording ('A, B fibres') is imprecise since GBS predominantly hits myelinated somatic (A) fibres, but among the choices it is the only one describing peripheral demyelination, so it is the intended answer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A video shows a 4-year-old boy asked to stand up from the floor: he rolls prone, pushes onto his hands and feet, then 'walks' his hands up his own thighs to reach standing. He has bulky calves and a waddling gait. This manoeuvre and the most likely inheritance pattern are:
questions.concept: Using the hands to 'climb up' the legs when rising is Gower's sign, indicating proximal (pelvic-girdle) weakness - classically Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy with absent dystrophin and calf pseudohypertrophy. A Trendelenburg sign reflects hip-abductor weakness; a Romberg sign reflects proprioceptive/dorsal-column loss.
questions.reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 21e / Harrison's 21e - Muscular Dystrophies

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: CSF shows abundant PMNs with low sugar and elevated protein. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: CSF with neutrophil (PMN) predominance, low glucose and high protein is typical of acute bacterial meningitis. Tubercular and fungal meningitis show lymphocytic predominance with low glucose, while viral meningitis has lymphocytes with normal glucose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young patient experiences shortness of breath specifically during exercise in winter, which subsides after using salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
options: Airway hyperreactivity due to cold-induced asthma exacerbation
Vagal stimulation due to cold air exposure
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction triggered by cold air
questions.concept: Exercise in cold, dry air causes airway heat/water loss and hyper-reactivity, triggering exercise-induced bronchoconstriction that reverses with an inhaled beta-2 agonist such as salbutamol. Exercise is the specific trigger here, distinguishing it from a general asthma exacerbation (option D is close but not exercise-specific).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient with asthma on inhaled corticosteroids and a LABA continues to have exacerbations. FEV1 is normal, there is no improvement with a salbutamol challenge, and symptoms worsen seasonally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.concept: In a patient still uncontrolled on ICS + LABA, the GINA approach is to first check adherence/technique/triggers and optimise anti-inflammatory control by stepping up the ICS dose before adding LAMA or biologics; omalizumab is reserved for severe allergic asthma failing maximal inhaled therapy. NOTE: management-step questions are guideline-dependent, but increasing ICS is the conventional next step here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: What is Zileuton's mechanism of action?
questions.concept: Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that blocks synthesis of leukotrienes from arachidonic acid, used to control asthma. COX inhibition describes NSAIDs, PDE-5 inhibition describes sildenafil, and mast-cell stabilisation describes cromolyn.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient presents with respiratory difficulty and a history of chronic smoking. Pulmonary function testing shows a decreased FEV1%. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: A chronic smoker with a reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC (<70%) has an obstructive pattern, most consistent with COPD. Fibrosis/ILD are restrictive (normal or high FEV1/FVC), and asthma is obstructive but reversible with bronchodilators.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the earliest sign of pregnancy on transvaginal sonography (TVS)?
questions.concept: On transvaginal ultrasound the earliest visible sign of intrauterine pregnancy is the gestational sac (from about 4.5-5 weeks), appearing before the yolk sac, fetal pole and cardiac activity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A primigravida at term has been in labour for several hours; over 4 hours the cervix remains at 6 cm with ruptured membranes. Contractions are infrequent and weak (2 in 10 minutes), there is no fetal distress and no evidence of cephalopelvic disproportion, but the cervicograph has crossed the alert line. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.concept: This is primary dysfunctional (hypotonic) labour - inadequate uterine activity with no CPD and a reassuring fetus - so oxytocin augmentation (with amniotomy if needed) is appropriate. Caesarean/forceps are not justified without CPD, fetal distress or a fully dilated cervix; simple observation would prolong an already abnormal labour.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: During assisted vaginal delivery, where is the vacuum device typically applied?
options: 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
Between the anterior and posterior fontanelle
At 3 cm behind the anterior fontanelle
questions.concept: The vacuum cup is placed over the flexion point, about 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle along the sagittal suture, so that traction flexes the fetal head and presents the smallest (suboccipitobregmatic) diameter, improving success and minimizing trauma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who delivered a healthy term baby one week ago presents with a fishy-smelling, pale-brownish vaginal discharge. What is the nature of this discharge?
questions.concept: Lochia serosa is the normal puerperal discharge from about days 5-9, appearing yellowish/pink/pale-brownish (fewer RBCs, more leukocytes and wound exudate); lochia rubra (days 1-4) is red and lochia alba (days 10-15) is pale-white. The mild fishy odour is normal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: All of the following are protected against by oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) EXCEPT?
questions.concept: Combined oral contraceptive pills reduce the risk of ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancers, but do NOT protect against - and may slightly increase - breast cancer risk, so breast carcinoma is the exception.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman requesting contraception has migraine WITH aura but no other risk factors. She is keen on the combined oral contraceptive pill. Which is the single most important reason to refuse the combined pill and offer an alternative?
options: Combined pills are simply less effective than a progestogen-only pill
Combined pills always cause weight gain in migraineurs
Combined (oestrogen-containing) pills are contraindicated - migraine with aura markedly increases ischaemic stroke risk
Combined pills reduce menstrual bleeding, which would mask her migraine
questions.concept: Migraine WITH aura is a WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria category 4 (unacceptable risk) condition for combined hormonal contraceptives because oestrogen further raises the already-elevated ischaemic stroke risk. Safer choices are progestogen-only methods, the copper IUCD or barrier methods. Efficacy and weight change are not the governing concern here.
questions.reference: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria 5e / DC Dutta's Gynaecology 7e (Contraception)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: OCPs are not protective for?
questions.concept: Combined OCPs reduce the risk of ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancers, but are not protective against breast cancer (slightly increased risk, as with cervical cancer).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: On ultrasound a placental mass is seen invading through the uterine wall into the urinary bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Placenta percreta is the most severe placenta-accreta-spectrum disorder, in which chorionic villi penetrate through the myometrium and serosa into an adjacent organ - here bladder invasion confirms percreta. Accreta is villi adherent to the myometrium and increta is invasion into (but not through) the myometrium; placenta previa is implantation over the cervical os and does not invade the bladder. (NOTE: the source listed 'placenta previa' twice; the duplicated 4th option has been corrected to the spectrum's missing 'placenta increta', which the source explanation itself defines.)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 34-week primigravida with known pre-eclampsia develops right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Investigations show haemolysis (schistocytes on smear, LDH 700 U/L), AST 150 U/L and a platelet count of 78,000/microL. What is the diagnosis and definitive management?
options: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura; give steroids and continue to term
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy; treat with antivirals
HELLP syndrome; stabilise the mother (including magnesium sulfate) and deliver
Gestational thrombocytopenia; reassure and continue pregnancy
questions.concept: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets in a pre-eclamptic woman define HELLP syndrome, a severe variant of pre-eclampsia. Definitive treatment is delivery after maternal stabilisation (control BP, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis). Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and isolated without haemolysis or liver derangement.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Obstetrics 9e (Hypertensive disorders - HELLP syndrome)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with irregular periods, acne and excessive hair growth. What is the first-line management?
questions.concept: Oligomenorrhoea, acne and hirsutism describe PCOS, and first-line management is lifestyle modification (weight reduction, diet and exercise), which improves ovulation and hyperandrogenism before adding drugs such as OCPs, metformin or clomiphene.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old raised as a girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has not developed breast tissue, ultrasound shows absence of the uterus, and karyotyping shows a 46,XY pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A 46,XY phenotypic girl with primary amenorrhoea, an absent uterus AND absent breast development points to 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency: functioning testes make AMH (no uterus) but the enzyme block halts both androgen and estrogen synthesis (no breasts), typically with hypertension and hypokalaemia. AIS would have breasts (androgens aromatized to estrogen) and Swyer's would have a uterus (streak gonads, no AMH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with infertility has severe secondary dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and cyclical painful defaecation. On examination the uterus is fixed and retroverted with tender nodules palpable in the pouch of Douglas along the uterosacral ligaments. What is the diagnosis and the gold-standard method to confirm it?
options: Endometriosis; confirmed by diagnostic laparoscopy with visualisation and biopsy
Pelvic inflammatory disease; confirmed by high vaginal swab culture
Ovarian carcinoma; confirmed by serum CA-125
questions.concept: Secondary dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia, infertility and tender uterosacral/pouch-of-Douglas nodules are classic for endometriosis; laparoscopy (with visualisation and histological confirmation) is the diagnostic gold standard. CA-125 may be raised but is non-specific, and endometrial biopsy diagnoses adenomyosis/endometrial pathology, not endometriosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which therapy is given for cervical cancer?
questions.concept: Locally advanced cervical cancer is treated with concurrent chemoradiation using cisplatin, a platinum-based drug, as the radiosensitiser; hormonal and targeted therapies are not the mainstay.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old multiparous woman with biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix has parametrial disease extending to the pelvic side wall. She now develops bilateral hydronephrosis with a rising serum creatinine. Which is the most common cause of death in advanced carcinoma cervix, exemplified by this patient?
options: Uraemia from bilateral ureteric obstruction (renal failure)
questions.concept: Carcinoma cervix spreads by direct/lateral extension into the parametrium and can encase both ureters, causing bilateral obstruction, hydronephrosis and death from uraemia (renal failure) - the classic commonest mode of death. Side-wall extension with hydronephrosis also defines advanced (stage IIIB) disease. Distant visceral metastases are comparatively late and less often the terminal event.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old obese, diabetic, nulliparous woman presents with painless postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Which diagnosis must be excluded first, and by which investigation?
options: Endometrial carcinoma; endometrial biopsy (with transvaginal USG)
questions.concept: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial carcinoma until proven otherwise. Risk factors include unopposed oestrogen, obesity, nulliparity, diabetes and late menopause. Evaluate with transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial thickness) and endometrial biopsy/sampling for a tissue diagnosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with weight loss and dyspepsia is found to have bilateral solid ovarian masses. Histology shows mucin-filled 'signet-ring' cells. The most likely primary site is:
questions.concept: Bilateral ovarian metastases with signet-ring cells define a Krukenberg tumour, most often from a gastric (or colonic) primary. It is a reminder to search for a gastrointestinal primary when ovarian masses are bilateral and mucin-secreting.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A pelvic ultrasound in a 55-year-old postmenopausal woman with abdominal distension shows a complex solid-cystic right adnexal mass with thick septations and papillary projections, ascites and omental 'caking'; serum CA-125 is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis and the commonest histological type?
options: Bilateral Krukenberg (metastatic) tumours from the stomach
Dysgerminoma - the commonest ovarian malignancy overall
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma - serous cystadenocarcinoma is the commonest type
questions.concept: A complex solid-cystic adnexal mass with ascites, omental caking and a high CA-125 in a postmenopausal woman is typical of epithelial ovarian carcinoma, of which serous cystadenocarcinoma is the commonest histological subtype. Dysgerminoma and granulosa cell tumours occur in younger women; Krukenberg tumours are characteristically bilateral with signet-ring cells from a GI primary.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Gynaecology 7e (Ovarian tumours) / Robbins Pathology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: What is the co-test in cervical cancer screening?
questions.concept: Co-testing in cervical cancer screening combines HPV DNA testing with the Pap smear (cytology); together they raise sensitivity, allowing 5-yearly screening in women aged 30-65 when negative. VIA is a low-resource alternative and colposcopy is a diagnostic follow-up, not a primary screening test.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman presents with irregular bleeding; endometrial biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the likely management?
questions.concept: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is treated with progestogens, and the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is first-line because it delivers sustained local progestogen with the best regression rates. Unopposed estradiol would worsen the hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman who had a forceps delivery 24 hours ago presents with perineal pain. Her BP is 80/60 and examination shows a swelling with bluish discolouration. Which of the following is advised NOT to do?
options: Repair the wound in the ward
questions.concept: A post-forceps vulvovaginal (paravaginal) haematoma with hypotension is an obstetric emergency; correct management is resuscitation with blood transfusion, informing seniors and evacuating the haematoma in the OT under anaesthesia. Opening/repairing it on the ward is what should NOT be done.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the following is not used in the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)?
questions.concept: Oxytocin, misoprostol (PGE1) and carboprost (15-methyl-PGF2-alpha) are standard uterotonics for PPH. Dinoprostone (PGE2) is used for cervical ripening/induction and mid-trimester abortion, not for PPH, as it is a vasodilator and a weak uterotonic at term.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, recurrent pregnancy loss
questions.stem: A primigravida has first-trimester vaginal bleeding; ultrasound shows a well-formed gestational sac with an embryo and present fetal cardiac activity. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.concept: First-trimester bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy (sac, embryo and fetal cardiac activity) and a closed cervix is a threatened abortion, which may still continue. Inevitable/incomplete abortion have an open cervix (with a low sac or retained products), and complete abortion shows an empty uterus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The development of cataracts in patients with diabetes mellitus is primarily due to the accumulation of which of the following substances in the lens?
questions.concept: In diabetes, excess glucose is reduced to sorbitol by aldose reductase (the polyol pathway); sorbitol is trapped in the lens, drawing in water (osmotic stress) and causing cataract. Dulcitol/galactitol accumulate in galactosaemia, not diabetes, and mannitol is an exogenous osmotic diuretic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly woman presents with sudden pain, redness and decreased vision. Examination shows a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: NOTE: the scraped key said A (acute uveitis) but that is wrong. A fixed mid-dilated pupil, a shallow anterior chamber and a hazy (oedematous) cornea with sudden pain in an elderly patient are the hallmark of acute angle-closure (congestive) glaucoma. Anterior uveitis instead gives a small/miotic or irregular pupil with a normal-depth chamber and keratic precipitates, so C is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A posterior staphyloma is observed on fundus examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia of the weakened, stretched posterior sclera at the posterior pole and is characteristic of pathological (degenerative) high myopia, in which progressive axial elongation thins the sclera, choroid and retina. Hypermetropia has a short axial length, and glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa do not cause scleral ectasia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 32-year-old patient presents with blurred vision, photophobia, and mild ocular pain. Examination reveals aqueous flares and keratic precipitates in the anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Keratic precipitates with aqueous flare and cells in the anterior chamber indicate anterior uveitis, i.e. iridocyclitis (inflammation of the iris and ciliary body); intermediate, posterior and toxoplasma uveitis instead involve the vitreous or chorioretina, not the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient presents with vision problems and has a history of cataract surgery. OCT finding is shown below. What is the syndrome most likely associated with these findings?
questions.concept: Reduced vision weeks to months after cataract surgery due to cystoid macular oedema (petaloid pattern on OCT/fluorescein angiography) is Irvine-Gass syndrome (pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema). It is distinct from central serous retinopathy and from posterior capsule opacification (Elschnig pearls).

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 23 year old male epileptic patient presented with pain in right shoulder region. Examination revealed that right upper limb was abducted and externally rotated and the movements could not be performed. Which of the following is most likely diagnosed?
questions.concept: An arm held abducted and externally rotated with loss of movement indicates an anterior shoulder dislocation, of which subglenoid is a variety. NOTE: the seizure history is a distractor pointing to posterior dislocation (which instead gives an adducted, internally rotated arm); the described position confirms an anterior/subglenoid dislocation.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A young adult presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.concept: In a young adult a femoral neck fracture is managed by urgent anatomical reduction and internal fixation to preserve the native femoral head and reduce avascular necrosis and non-union; arthroplasty (hemi or total) is reserved for elderly or low-demand patients with displaced fractures.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: According to WHO, which of the following is the recommended diagnostic test for spinal tuberculosis?
questions.concept: WHO now recommends rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF, i.e. CBNAAT) as the initial diagnostic test for all forms of tuberculosis, including spinal/extrapulmonary disease. NOTE: the scraped key said D (culture); culture remains the microbiological gold standard, so the item is genuinely ambiguous between the WHO-recommended initial test (CBNAAT) and the gold standard (culture) - flagged.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a progressively increasing swelling over the tibia along with fever. Radiological examination reveals a Codman triangle and sunburst appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A Codman triangle with a sunburst/sunray periosteal reaction in an adolescent's long-bone metaphysis (around the knee) is classic for osteosarcoma; Ewing sarcoma typically shows an onion-skin reaction and giant cell tumour is epiphyseal and lytic.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: An investigator compares the mean blood pressure (with standard deviations) between two independent groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
questions.concept: Comparing the means of two independent groups of continuous, approximately normal data uses the unpaired (independent-samples) t-test. The paired t-test is for matched/before-after data, chi-square is for categorical associations, and ANOVA compares means of more than two groups.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A researcher compares the mean fasting blood glucose across THREE independent groups (drug A, drug B, placebo); within each group the values are approximately normally distributed with similar variances. Which statistical test is most appropriate to test whether the three group means differ?
questions.concept: Comparing the means of THREE or more independent, normally distributed groups uses one-way ANOVA; running multiple t-tests instead inflates the type-I error rate. The chi-square test is for categorical/proportional data, and a paired t-test is for two related (before-after) measurements on the same subjects.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the management of a HIV positive patient with multiple dog bites?
questions.concept: Multiple bites are Category III exposure, and an immunocompromised (HIV-positive) patient must receive full post-exposure prophylaxis: thorough wound washing PLUS rabies vaccine PLUS rabies immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A person living with HIV (PLHIV) presents with multiple dog bites with a punctured (deep) wound. Choose the correct management:
questions.concept: A category III rabies exposure (bleeding/deep bites), and any exposure in an immunocompromised person such as a PLHIV, requires the full regimen: thorough wound washing plus rabies immunoglobulin (RIG - human 20 IU/kg or equine 40 IU/kg, infiltrated around the wound) plus the anti-rabies vaccine series.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Marriage and mortality belong under?
questions.concept: Fertility, mortality, migration and marriage are the demographic processes that determine population size and structure; demographic dividend/bonus/window instead describe the economic benefit of a large working-age population.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a family with three siblings, the eldest sibling moves out of the household and a new (third) child is born. What is this change in the family structure called?
questions.concept: In the family life cycle, extension is the phase of adding members (births) while contraction is losing them (children leaving). NOTE: this scenario mixes both (the eldest leaves while a new child is born) and the source's definition of 'complete extension' (multi-generational overlap) is non-standard, so the mapping is genuinely ambiguous. Keyed answer C retained but flagged for review.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a demographic report a country has a Net Reproduction Rate (NRR) of exactly 1.0. What does this value indicate about the population's long-term replacement?
options: Each generation of mothers is exactly replaced by one surviving daughter (replacement level)
The population will double within one generation
The crude birth rate equals the crude death rate this year
The total fertility rate must be zero
questions.concept: The NRR is the average number of daughters a woman would bear who survive to reproductive age, allowing for mortality. An NRR of 1 is exactly replacement level (each mother replaced by one surviving daughter); above 1 means growth and below 1 means eventual decline. It is not the same as equal crude birth and death rates in a single year.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of PSM 27e - Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: What does the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) primarily indicate in water quality management?
questions.concept: The Langelier Saturation Index indicates whether water tends to deposit calcium carbonate scale (positive LSI) or dissolve it and corrode pipes (negative LSI), with zero being balanced; it is derived from pH, alkalinity, hardness and temperature. It does not measure TDS or biological contamination.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A photograph shows colour-coded biomedical-waste bins in a hospital operating under India's Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. Used needles, syringes with fixed needles and scalpel blades (sharps) should be discarded into which colour-coded, puncture-proof container?
questions.concept: VERIFY: confirm against the CURRENT Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 (as amended) colour code before trusting this key, as categories are policy-set and periodically revised. As authored: sharps (needles, blades) go to a WHITE translucent puncture-proof container; yellow = anatomical/soiled/pathological waste; red = contaminated recyclable plastics (tubing, IV sets); blue = discarded glassware and metallic implants.
questions.reference: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (India) - CONFIRM current amended schedule

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A gym owner observes that individuals who drink iced tea during their workouts tend to lose more weight. What is the nature of this relationship?
questions.concept: This is an indirect association: the real association is entirely explained by a common confounder (the exercise/health-consciousness that accompanies iced-tea drinking drives the weight loss), so iced tea is not the direct cause. A spurious association would be a false one arising from chance or bias.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a study based in Delhi, doctors followed 100 people who did exercise for a year and later they checked who all had developed coronary heart disease. Which type of study is this?
questions.concept: Following a defined exposed group (exercisers) forward over time to see who develops the outcome (coronary heart disease) is a cohort study - it moves from exposure to outcome. Because follow-up runs forward it is also 'prospective', but the study TYPE being asked for is cohort.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A study used office records over the past 20 years to compare the incidence of disease among factory workers exposed to aniline dye versus unexposed clerical staff. What type of epidemiological study is this?
questions.concept: Grouping subjects by exposure (aniline dye vs clerical) and tracing disease incidence through already-existing past records is a retrospective (historical) cohort study - both exposure and outcome had occurred before the study began. Case-control starts from disease status, not exposure; ecological uses population-level not individual data.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: On 1 January 2024, an area of 10,000 people had 100 TB cases. During the year 30 were cured, 10 died, 20 new cases occurred, and 5 of the new cases were cured by 31 December. What are the incidence and prevalence of TB (per 1,000 and %, respectively)?
questions.concept: Incidence counts only new cases among those at risk: 20/(10,000-100) x 1,000 = about 2 per 1,000. Period prevalence counts all cases during the interval: (100 existing + 20 new)/10,000 = 1.2%. NOTE: the source's route (75/10,000 = 0.75% ~ 1.2%) is arithmetically wrong; 1.2% is correctly the period prevalence, and the option mixes units (per-1,000 for incidence, % for prevalence).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A total of 60 patients were diagnosed with COVID-19, of which 12 deaths were reported. Calculate the case fatality rate.
questions.concept: Case fatality rate = (deaths from a disease / diagnosed cases of that disease) x 100 = 12/60 x 100 = 20%. It measures the lethality of a disease among diagnosed cases.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a class of 100 students, 80% students were immunised with measles, 12 were affected. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.concept: Secondary attack rate = new cases among susceptible contacts / total susceptible contacts x 100. With 80 of 100 immunised, only 20 are susceptible; 12 cases give SAR = 12/20 = 60%.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A study analysed how much time nursing staff spend on different tasks (bed preparation, monitoring vitals, doctor's rounds, blood sampling, drug administration) by observing them at random intervals. Which management technique is most appropriate?
questions.concept: Sampling activities at random moments to estimate the proportion of time spent on each task is Work Sampling. A Time and Motion study instead times each step continuously, the Critical Path Method schedules dependent project tasks, and systems analysis studies whole processes.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A long-term study found that individuals who had high blood pressure (BP) during childhood continued to have high BP in adulthood, and those with low BP in childhood tended to maintain lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best represent?
questions.concept: Tracking describes the tendency of an individual to keep their relative rank within a population distribution over time, so a child at the high end of BP stays high as an adult. It differs from regression to the mean (extreme values drifting toward the average on re-measurement) and the cohort effect (differences between people born in different periods).

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following is the formula for sensitivity?
questions.concept: Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) x 100, i.e. the proportion of truly diseased people the test correctly identifies. TP/(TP+FP) is positive predictive value and TN/(TN+FP) is specificity.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Between the MR and Pentavalent vaccines, which can be reused and which must be discarded once the vial is opened, per the open vial policy?
questions.concept: The Pentavalent vaccine is a preserved liquid multi-dose vial eligible for the open vial policy (reusable up to 28 days if the cold chain and VVM are intact). The MR vaccine is a reconstituted lyophilised vaccine without preservative and must be discarded within a few hours of reconstitution. So: discard MR, reuse Pentavalent.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Iron absorption is decreased in which of the following?
questions.concept: Tannins/polyphenols in tea (and coffee) chelate non-haem iron and reduce its absorption, whereas the vitamin C in amla, lemon and sprouted grains enhances iron absorption.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme), which diseases are covered under sentinel surveillance?
questions.concept: Under India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), sentinel surveillance targets the bloodborne infections HIV and Hepatitis B (and C) through designated sentinel sites/blood banks, complementing regular and outbreak surveillance.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A factory worker sustained burns over 25% of his body on duty and later developed infections and complications. Under the ESI Act, which benefit is he eligible for?
questions.concept: Under the ESI Act, Extended Sickness Benefit covers insured workers with specified long-term diseases needing prolonged treatment, payable up to 2 years at about 140% of the standard rate. NOTE: eligibility requires the condition to be on the list of specified diseases, so the burns-complication link is a somewhat niche interpretation. Ordinary Sickness Benefit runs only ~91 days; Enhanced is for sterilisation; Dependants' is for death from employment injury.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 10-year-old child weighs 40 kg and has intellectual disability. The upper segment to lower segment (US:LS) ratio is 1.1:1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: The source keys rickets, arguing that an elevated US:LS ratio (1.1:1 vs the normal ~1.0 at age 10) reflects a shortened lower segment from long-bone disease. NOTE: this is disputed - rickets does not cause intellectual disability, whereas cretinism/congenital hypothyroidism classically gives BOTH an increased US:LS ratio AND mental retardation, so options A (cretinism) and D (hypothyroidism) are the stronger clinical fit and overlap with each other. Flagged for review.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: While evaluating a 3-year-old with short stature, height is measured at 90cm and the lower segment is 45 cm. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Height 90 cm with a lower segment of 45 cm gives an upper:lower segment ratio of 1:1, well below the roughly 1.3:1 expected at 3 years, indicating a short trunk. Short-trunk (reduced upper segment) dwarfism points to spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, whereas achondroplasia produces short limbs (a high US:LS ratio).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child with diarrhea was eager to drink, and the skin pinch went back slowly. Which of the following categories is the child classified into as per IMNCI?
questions.concept: A child who is restless/eager to drink with a skin pinch that goes back slowly has 'some dehydration', which is the Yellow IMNCI category (needs ORS/facility treatment); severe dehydration (lethargic, drinking poorly, very slow pinch) is Pink and no dehydration is Green.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An unimmunized 4-year-old has high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, with tiny bluish-white spots on an erythematous buccal mucosa, followed by a maculopapular rash that spreads from the face downward. Which statement is correct?
options: The buccal spots are Koplik spots (pathognomonic of measles); the first measles-rubella dose is due at 9 months
These are Forchheimer spots of rubella; the vaccine is given at birth
This is roseola and measles vaccine is given only at 5 years
This is scarlet fever and no vaccine exists
questions.concept: Koplik spots (grey-white spots on a red buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic of measles and precede the cephalocaudal maculopapular rash. In the Indian schedule the first measles-rubella (MR) dose is given at 9 completed months (second at 16-24 months). Pneumonia is the commonest cause of measles death.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e / UIP schedule - web-verified 2026-07-04

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: An unimmunised 5-year-old has a sore throat, low-grade fever and a greyish adherent membrane over the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when scraped, together with marked 'bull-neck' cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the causative organism and its most dangerous systemic complication?
questions.concept: A bleeding, adherent grey pseudomembrane with a 'bull neck' in an unimmunised child is diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae). Its exotoxin causes myocarditis (the leading cause of death) and neuropathy such as palatal palsy; treatment is prompt antitoxin plus antibiotics. Forcible removal of the membrane causes bleeding, a useful distinguishing clue.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn of a diabetic mother is symptomatic at 24 hours of life with a blood glucose <35 mg/dL. What is the next best step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.concept: A symptomatic neonate with glucose <35-40 mg/dL needs immediate IV 10% dextrose (about 2 mL/kg bolus) followed by a glucose infusion, with a recheck in 20-30 minutes. Infants of diabetic mothers are prone to hypoglycaemia from fetal hyperinsulinism. Oral feeds/observation suit only mild asymptomatic cases; Hartmann's has no glucose.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, high alkaline phosphatase and eosinophilic PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules on liver biopsy (suggestive of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency). What is the most common cause of jaundice in this setting?
questions.concept: Idiopathic neonatal hepatitis is the classic most common cause of neonatal conjugated hyperbilirubinemia/cholestasis (intrahepatic cholestasis, giant-cell change), and the PAS-positive globules point to alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency as the specific etiology. NOTE: biliary atresia is the main competing answer (commonest surgical cause) and physiological jaundice is unconjugated - hence moderate confidence.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A newborn child is brought to the emergency department with respiratory difficulty. The doctor evaluated, and the child was found to have a posterolateral defect, as shown in the x-ray given. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A neonate with respiratory distress and a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect has a Bochdalek hernia, the commonest congenital diaphragmatic hernia (about 90%), usually left-sided and often complicated by pulmonary hypoplasia. Morgagni hernia is retrosternal/anterior.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate on examination has bilateral cataracts and, after investigations, is found to have a patent ductus arteriosus and salt & pepper retinopathy. What is the most likely congenital infection?
questions.concept: The triad of bilateral cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus and 'salt-and-pepper' retinopathy is classic congenital rubella syndrome (first-trimester infection); sensorineural deafness is the commonest defect. CMV instead causes periventricular calcification and chorioretinitis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate has intestines protruding from the abdomen without any external covering. What is the next line of management?
options: Cover the content with a Silo bag and wait
questions.concept: Bowel protruding with no covering membrane is gastroschisis; when the abdominal cavity is too small for the oedematous bowel, the viscera are placed in a sterile silo and reduced in stages over several days before closure, avoiding abdominal compartment syndrome. (Omphalocele differs by having a peritoneal-amniotic sac.)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: When is a blood sample taken to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.concept: Newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism (heel-prick dried blood spot for TSH/T4) is done at about 48-72 hours of life; sampling in the first 24-48 h is avoided because of the physiological neonatal TSH surge, and cord blood is used only for universal screening.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Which of the following is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Giving a bath immediately after birth
Placing the baby on the mother's chest
Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
questions.concept: Bathing a newborn immediately after birth causes hypothermia, removes the protective vernix caseosa and delays skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding; WHO advises delaying the first bath at least 24 hours. Eye care, early breastfeeding and skin-to-skin contact are all beneficial.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A neonate was born to a controlled gestational diabetes mother. At the time of birth, he was fine but 4 days later, he developed dyspnea with SpO2 80% at room air. What is the initial management?
questions.concept: A term neonate who becomes cyanotic on day 4 may have cyanotic congenital heart disease or lung disease; giving 100% oxygen (the hyperoxia test) distinguishes them, as PaO2 rises to at least 100 mmHg with lung disease but fails to rise with a cardiac right-to-left shunt. NOTE: 100% O2 here is a diagnostic first step, and oxygen must be used cautiously if a duct-dependent lesion is suspected.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Normal parents have a first child with rickets. During preconception counselling, what are the chances of the second child getting it?
questions.concept: Two phenotypically normal (carrier) parents with an affected child indicate autosomal recessive inheritance (e.g., vitamin D-dependent rickets), giving a 25% recurrence risk in each subsequent pregnancy (with 50% carriers and 25% unaffected).

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 14-month-old exclusively breastfed child with minimal sun exposure has bow legs, a rachitic rosary, widened wrists, a delayed anterior fontanelle closure and delayed dentition. Wrist X-ray shows cupping and fraying of the metaphyses. Which deficiency is responsible and what is the characteristic biochemistry?
options: Vitamin C deficiency; normal alkaline phosphatase with subperiosteal haemorrhage
Vitamin A deficiency; hypercalcaemia with normal phosphate
Vitamin K deficiency; low alkaline phosphatase with bleeding
Vitamin D deficiency; low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone
questions.concept: Bow legs, rachitic rosary, widened wrists with metaphyseal cupping/fraying and delayed fontanelle closure define nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency (breastfed, low sun exposure). Biochemistry: low/normal calcium, low phosphate, HIGH alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Scurvy (vitamin C) causes bleeding with a normal ALP.
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e (Vitamin D deficiency / rickets)

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with severe acute malnutrition (weight-for-height below -3 SD with bilateral pitting pedal oedema) is admitted lethargic and cold to touch. During the initial stabilisation phase of WHO-based management, which pair of complications is the most important immediate threat to prevent?
questions.concept: In severe acute malnutrition the early killers are hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration and infection; management begins with frequent feeds, keeping the child warm, and treating/anticipating infection. High-protein diets and iron are deliberately withheld in the stabilisation phase (iron can worsen infection and free-radical injury; over-rapid feeding risks refeeding syndrome).
questions.reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e / WHO 10 steps for severe acute malnutrition

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has had sleep disturbance, low mood and stress for 3 months, which he attributes to ongoing problems at work. He has no prior psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Emotional symptoms arising within 3 months of an identifiable, non-traumatic stressor (work pressure) and not meeting criteria for another disorder define adjustment disorder. GAD requires excessive worry for at least 6 months, whereas acute stress disorder and PTSD both require exposure to a genuinely traumatic event.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher believes that all her students are failing because of her. She also reports hearing voices commenting on her actions. What is the best treatment?
questions.concept: Mood-congruent guilt delusions plus auditory hallucinations indicate major depression with psychotic features, best treated with an antidepressant PLUS an antipsychotic (or ECT in severe/refractory cases); an antidepressant alone is inadequate for the psychotic component.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A patient shows flat affect. What does it indicate?
questions.concept: Flat (blunted) affect is a negative symptom of schizophrenia, along with alogia, avolition and anhedonia. Positive symptoms are hallucinations and delusions.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: What is the diagnosis for a patient who believes their bodily sensations or movements are controlled or influenced by an external agency?
questions.concept: Somatic passivity - the delusion that one's bodily sensations or movements are imposed by an external agency - is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom of schizophrenia. Nihilistic delusion is belief that oneself/a body part does not exist; delusion of reference is that events refer to oneself; Othello syndrome is delusional jealousy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A person has a false belief that he owns a great deal of property and that someone he knows is trying to take it from him. Which delusions is he experiencing?
questions.concept: An exaggerated false belief about one's wealth/importance is a grandiose delusion, while the belief that someone is conspiring to harm or rob him is a persecutory delusion. A delusion of reference (neutral events aimed at oneself) and a nihilistic delusion (self/world does not exist) are not described here.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.stem: A doctor asked the patient what her age is and she told him that she is married to an older man, and she has 2 kids of 15 and 18 years, and she is 39 years old. What is the disorder present?
questions.concept: When asked her age the patient supplies many unnecessary details but eventually reaches the correct answer; this over-inclusive yet goal-directed speech is circumstantiality. In tangentiality or derailment the patient never returns to the point.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presented with severe abdominal pain following alcohol intake. Make a diagnosis based on the given X-ray.
questions.concept: Free gas under the diaphragm on an erect film indicates pneumoperitoneum, most often from a perforated peptic ulcer - a recognised cause of sudden severe abdominal pain in a patient after alcohol. NOTE: this is an image-dependent question and the X-ray itself was not available to review; the answer follows the scraped key and the text (abdominal, not chest, pain favours perforated ulcer over Boerhaave-related pneumomediastinum), so it is left unverified.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the investigation of choice for spinal TB?
questions.concept: MRI is the imaging investigation of choice for spinal tuberculosis (Pott's spine): it best demonstrates early marrow oedema, paravertebral/epidural abscesses and cord compression before bony changes appear on X-ray or CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Radioisotope used in PET-CT scan?
questions.concept: PET-CT most commonly uses 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), a positron-emitting glucose analogue that accumulates in metabolically active tissue such as malignant tumours.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Ga-68 PSMA PET scan is used to diagnose which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: Ga-68 PSMA (prostate-specific membrane antigen) PET/CT targets PSMA that is over-expressed on prostate cancer cells, and is used to stage and detect biochemically recurrent prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: What does a linear accelerator (LINAC) produce for radiation therapy?
questions.concept: A LINAC accelerates electrons to high energy; these electrons can treat superficial tumours directly or strike a target to generate high-energy X-rays (photons) for deep tumours - so it produces X-rays and electrons. Gamma rays come from radioactive isotopes (e.g., cobalt-60), not from a LINAC.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of lower right abdominal pain with rebound tenderness in a patient who also has a Meckel's diverticulum?
questions.concept: Right-lower-quadrant pain with rebound tenderness (localised peritonism at McBurney's point) points to acute appendicitis; even when a Meckel's diverticulum is present, this classic localising sign indicates appendicitis rather than diverticular perforation or obstruction, which cause more diffuse or colicky pain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation, develops sudden severe, diffuse abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to a soft, minimally tender abdomen. Over the next hours he passes bloody diarrhoea and develops a rising serum lactate with metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (superior mesenteric artery embolism)
questions.concept: Pain out of proportion to examination findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation, progressing to bloody stool and lactic (metabolic) acidosis, is classic for acute mesenteric ischaemia, usually an SMA embolism from the fibrillating atrium. A perforated ulcer gives early board-like rigidity, not a deceptively soft abdomen.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (Intestinal ischaemia / the acute abdomen)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
questions.concept: Intraductal papilloma, a benign growth within a lactiferous duct, is the commonest cause of bloody (or serosanguineous) nipple discharge; carcinoma and duct ectasia can also bleed but are less common.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman, 10 years after mastectomy, notices gradual swelling and heaviness in her right upper limb without pain. On examination, bluish nodules on the skin with no infections are noted. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.concept: Long-standing post-mastectomy lymphoedema of the arm that later develops bluish/purple cutaneous nodules is Stewart-Treves syndrome - a lymphangiosarcoma arising within the chronically lymphoedematous limb.

questions.subject: Surgery
