questions.stem: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth that has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A congenital (since-birth) inguinoscrotal swelling that turns irreducible, red and painful indicates a strangulated inguinal hernia, where trapped bowel has lost its blood supply - a surgical emergency. An incarcerated hernia is irreducible but still viable, without redness or severe tenderness.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: An elderly woman with a small femoral hernia develops fever and localized tenderness over the lump, but continues to pass stool and flatus with no abdominal distension. At operation only part of the circumference of the bowel wall (the antimesenteric border) is trapped and gangrenous. This is best described as:
questions.concept: In a Richter's hernia only part of the bowel-wall circumference is trapped, so it can strangulate and become gangrenous WITHOUT features of intestinal obstruction, a dangerous pitfall classically seen with femoral hernias. Littre's = Meckel's diverticulum in the sac; Maydl's = a W-shaped loop.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which of the following is the classical triad of acute cholangitis?
questions.concept: Charcot's triad of acute cholangitis is fever (with rigors), jaundice and right-upper-quadrant pain; adding hypotension/shock and altered mental status makes Reynolds' pentad, indicating acute obstructive suppurative cholangitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with known gallstones develops right upper quadrant pain, high fever with rigors and jaundice, and then becomes hypotensive and confused. What is the diagnosis, and after resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics, what is the definitive intervention?
options: Uncomplicated acute cholecystitis; interval cholecystectomy in 6 weeks only
Acute viral hepatitis; supportive management alone
Acute cholangitis; urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP
Amoebic liver abscess; oral metronidazole alone
questions.concept: Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever/rigors, jaundice) progressing to hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad) indicates acute cholangitis from an obstructed, infected biliary tree. After resuscitation and antibiotics, the definitive step is urgent biliary decompression/drainage, usually by ERCP. Delaying to a purely elective plan is inappropriate for a septic patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient develops muscle cramps, tetany, and carpopedal spasm after thyroid surgery. Which electrolyte imbalance is responsible?
questions.concept: Muscle cramps, tetany and carpopedal spasm (Trousseau/Chvostek positive) after thyroid surgery reflect hypocalcaemia from inadvertent removal of or damage to the parathyroid glands, reducing PTH and hence serum calcium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: About 24 hours after a total thyroidectomy, a woman develops circumoral and fingertip tingling and painful carpopedal spasm. Tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the facial muscles. What is the most likely cause and the immediate management?
options: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy; immediate re-exploration
Hypocalcaemia from inadvertent parathyroid injury/removal; give intravenous calcium gluconate
questions.concept: Perioral/peripheral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm and a positive Chvostek's sign after total thyroidectomy indicate acute HYPOCALCAEMIA from damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands; management is intravenous calcium gluconate (with later oral calcium/vitamin D). Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes voice/airway problems, not tetany.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (The thyroid gland - complications of thyroidectomy)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 30-year-old with a firm thyroid nodule reports episodic headaches, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension, and has a family history of thyroid cancer. FNAC shows tumour cells in an amyloid stroma and serum calcitonin is markedly raised. What is the diagnosis, and which coexisting tumour must be excluded before any thyroid surgery?
options: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma; proceed straight to surgery
Papillary thyroid carcinoma; no additional work-up needed
Medullary thyroid carcinoma (part of MEN 2A); exclude and treat a phaeochromocytoma first
questions.concept: Amyloid-containing FNAC with a high calcitonin indicates medullary thyroid carcinoma (from parafollicular C cells), here within MEN 2A. A coexisting phaeochromocytoma MUST be excluded (metanephrines) and, if present, resected FIRST - operating on the thyroid before controlling the phaeochromocytoma risks a fatal hypertensive crisis.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 27e (The thyroid gland - medullary carcinoma / MEN 2)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the ER 6 hours after a burn, with 22% BSA burns. On examination: cool extremities, BP 92/50 mmHg, PR 56 bpm, urine output since the burn 30 mL. What is the next step in management?
questions.concept: This child with over 15% BSA burns and shock (hypotension, cool peripheries, low urine output and ominous bradycardia) needs an urgent crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) bolus, about 10 mL/kg, before calculated Parkland resuscitation; colloids are avoided in the first 24 hours because of capillary leak, and a 30 mL/kg bolus risks fluid overload. (The bolus wording in the recall is imprecise.)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A patient underwent split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury on the arm. On post-operative day 6 he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.concept: On post-op day 6 a split-thickness graft is still only loosely adherent during early revascularisation, so joint stiffness should be addressed by gentle passive extension under direct visualisation of the graft to avoid shearing it off. Contracture excision or regrafting are not indicated this early.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 25-year-old trauma victim has a heart rate of 130/min, a measurable fall in systolic blood pressure, respiratory rate of 30/min, confusion and reduced urine output. Using the ATLS classification, this corresponds to approximately which class and volume of blood loss?
questions.concept: Hypotension with marked tachycardia (120-140/min), tachypnoea and altered mental status defines Class III haemorrhagic shock (30-40% blood loss, ~1.5-2 L), the point at which blood pressure clearly falls. Class II has tachycardia with still-normal BP; Class IV is >40% with obtundation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A newborn male presents with urinary retention, lethargy and a distended bladder. Antenatal ultrasound showed a 'keyhole sign' with a thickened bladder wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A newborn boy with a distended, thick-walled bladder, urinary retention and an antenatal 'keyhole sign' (dilated bladder plus dilated posterior urethra) has posterior urethral valves, the commonest cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy has sudden severe left testicular pain of 3 hours' duration with nausea. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and is exquisitely tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on that side. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Scrotal support and analgesia with review in 48 hours
Doppler ultrasound and reassess the following morning
Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy
questions.concept: Sudden pain with a high-riding, horizontal, tender testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion - a surgical emergency requiring IMMEDIATE exploration and bilateral orchidopexy, since the testis is best salvaged within about 6 hours. When the picture is classic, do not delay for imaging; epididymo-orchitis is a dangerous misdiagnosis here.
